breakdown.deepRead:
Grace faces the same pattern in microbrewery partnership replacing a childhood friend in the accounts role. The useful distinction is friendship blur, enemy incentive, envy. Apply the move through the setup, not through a generic speech.
Michael III trusted the emotional comfort of friendship and missed the appetite growing beside him. Basilius did not become dangerous because friendship was always false. He became dangerous because affection blurred the line between gratitude and entitlement once power opened a door. That is the warning: a friend can carry old emotional claims into a new role, while an enemy may bring cleaner incentives because both sides know what must be watched.
A former rival can be safer than a beloved friend when the terms are visible. The rival has something to prove, something to gain, and less room to hide behind intimacy. The friend may expect forgiveness, exception, or permanent access. The question is not who feels warmer. The question is whose incentives can be read before the decision hardens.
breakdown.fullRead:
Rachel sees the limit clearly in community legal clinic using a former opponent on a zoning appeal. The move helps only when it stays narrower than never trust friends and only trust enemies. If it becomes a pose, it loses the practical force that made it useful.
Talleyrand and Fouche worked from the clarity of mutual caution, not the fog of sentiment. Each man understood that the other was capable, dangerous, and useful under the right terms. That kind of alliance can be more legible than friendship because suspicion keeps the arrangement awake. Nobody has to pretend that affection has erased ambition.
The practical test is simple: can you name what this person gains by helping you, and can they name what they lose by betraying the arrangement? If the answer is clearer with an old enemy than with an old friend, warmth may be the less reliable guide. Use affection where it belongs, but do not let it replace structure.
